[Lesson 03 / Fourier heat flow]{.lesson-kicker}

# Same heat, different derivative

[What if the spatial derivative is already exact for our wave, but the answer still has an error?]{.lesson-deck}

:::

In the [previous lesson](../finite-differences/index.qmd), a finite stencil
approximated curvature. Here we change that one numerical choice. The
periodic domain, initial condition, physical right-hand side, and Euler
update remain the same. This refactors the former
`20_explicit_stepper_spectral.cpp` around an independently checkable field.

## A heat equation in Fourier space

For the periodic problem on $[0,2\pi)^3$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\partial_t u=D\Delta u, \\
u(\mathbf{x},0)=1+0.2\cos x\cos y\cos z,
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-heat}

write a trigonometric interpolant
$u_N(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\widehat u_{\mathbf{k}}
e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}$. Its Laplacian is

$$
\widehat{\Delta u}_{\mathbf{k}}=-|\mathbf{k}|^2\widehat u_{\mathbf{k}}.
$$ {#eq-symbol}

Differentiation becomes multiplication by a known symbol. The constant
mode has $\mathbf{k}=0$ and remains unchanged. Each nonconstant mode in
our initial condition has $|\mathbf{k}|^2=3$.

These modes are represented exactly on our grid. Fourier differentiation
therefore introduces no truncation error for this particular field, apart
from roundoff. That property belongs to a resolved trigonometric mode;
it does not mean the method exactly differentiates every smooth function
at a finite resolution [@trefethen2000, programs 1 and 5].

## Change the stack, keep the equation

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="initialize" dedent=4}
```

Compare the initialisation with the FD lesson. `SpectralCPUStack` sizes the
field to the FFT's local real-space box. Its evaluator transforms the
field and applies @eq-symbol for the requested second derivatives.
There is no face-halo exchange in this implementation.

The physical update stays the same:

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="evolve" dedent=4}
```

The physics still reads $D(u_{xx}+u_{yy}+u_{zz})$. Keeping that expression
visible makes the boundary between physical law and numerical method easy
to inspect.

## Why is there still an error?

The exact mode amplitude is $A(t)=0.2e^{-3Dt}$. Euler instead gives

$$
A_n=0.2(1-3D\Delta t)^n.
$$ {#eq-amplitude}

At a fixed final time, this is a first-order approximation in $\Delta t$.
Increasing $N$ cannot fix it. Halving $\Delta t$ should roughly halve the
error once the asymptotic regime is reached.

Stability also belongs to the time integrator. On an even grid the most
negative Laplacian symbol is $-3(\pi/h)^2$. Euler requires

$$
\Delta t\le\frac{2h^2}{3D\pi^2}.
$$ {#eq-stability}

This bound is stricter than the second-order FD bound. Although our
initial field contains only low modes, the executable enforces the bound
for the complete represented spectrum, including perturbations introduced
by roundoff.

![The same heat problem under finite differences, Fourier-Euler, and exponential Fourier evolution. The Fourier-Euler error persists despite exact spatial representation of the initial mode.](../figures/methods.svg){#fig-methods}

## Try the experiment

From `examples/heat/fourier`:

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --source-root .. --launcher=none
```

Inspect the printed attempt's `results/diagnostics.csv` and final field
CSVs. The columns and exact solution are the same as in the FD lesson.
The source is [model.cpp](model.cpp); parameters are in [input.json](input.json).

First change `n` from 16 to 32, keeping `dt` and `steps` fixed. The
continuum error should be almost unchanged. Then return to `n=16`, halve
`dt`, and double `steps`: the final time stays fixed while the temporal
error decreases.

A useful wrong expectation is that a finer spectral grid permits a larger
explicit timestep. Try `n=64` with the original `dt=0.001`. The input
should be rejected by @eq-stability. Explain why resolving shorter waves
makes this explicit method more restrictive.

## Verification and scope

The example checks reconstruct the entire field from @eq-amplitude,
independently of OpenPFC's FFT routines. They also check the zero mode,
RMS decay, continuum error, invalid inputs, and one versus two MPI ranks.
This chapter covers a periodic linear equation on the CPU. It introduces
neither nonlinear dealiasing nor nonperiodic boundary conditions.

The [next lesson](../exponential/index.qmd) removes Euler's approximation
by solving each linear Fourier-mode equation analytically.

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson. It also uses the shared [lesson.hpp](../lesson.hpp);
keep its relative location when saving the files.
